stages.title: Ecclesiastical Latin
stages.summary: The Latin of the Bible and of the Fathers who read it.
stages.statusNote: Populated from the Clementine Vulgate, Tertullian, Cyprian, Augustine and Cassian. The library does not yet hold Latin hymns, Ambrose, or Jerome's own letters and prefaces, so those parts of the stage are not taught.

units.title: The Latin Bible
units.summary: What makes the Vulgate's Latin its own.

lessons.title: Reading the Psalms and the Gospels in Latin

stages.title: Medieval and Scholastic Latin
stages.statusNote: The stage is defined (medieval vocabulary and spelling, scholastic terminology, and the article structure of Aquinas: objections, sed contra, respondeo, replies) but has no lessons: the library holds Anselm, Bernard, Aquinas and Bonaventure in English only. It needs a public-domain Latin text of each (for Aquinas, one that marks the parts of an article) and a linguistic analysis of it.

stages.title: Reformation and Early Modern Latin
stages.statusNote: Defined but without lessons: the library holds no Latin text of Erasmus, Luther, Melanchthon, Calvin or Turretin. It needs public-domain Latin editions and their analysis.

stages.title: Independent Advanced Latin Reading
stages.summary: Choosing a whole work and reading it through.
stages.statusNote: Independent reading is supported for the Latin works the library holds with analysis: the whole Vulgate, the Confessions, Cassian's Institutes, Cyprian, Tertullian and Augustine On the Spirit and the Letter. Scholastic and Reformation works await their Latin texts.

units.title: Whole works
units.summary: Method and a first whole book.

objectives.can: Read Latin letters aloud in the classical or the ecclesiastical pronunciation, and say where the two differ.
Divide a Latin word into syllables and place its accent by the rule of the penult.
Find the verb, its subject and its object in a short Latin sentence by their endings, not their position.
Tell a nominative from an accusative and say which is subject and which is object.
Recognise ten of the commonest nouns of the Latin Bible.
Recognise genitive and dative forms and give the commonest sense of each.
Recognise ten more common nouns.
Recognise the ablative and its main uses, and the vocative.
Parse and form nouns of the first and second declensions.
Recognise ten common first- and second-declension nouns.
Parse third-declension nouns and find the stem from the genitive.
Recognise ten common third-declension nouns.
Parse nouns of the fourth and fifth declensions.
Match an adjective to its noun in case, number and gender, whatever their declensions.
Recognise ten common adjectives.
Say which case a preposition takes and what the commonest conjunctions join.
Recognise the commonest prepositions and conjunctions.
Parse the forms of ego, tu, nos, vos and the forms of is used for 'he, she, it'.
Parse the present, imperfect and future indicative of sum.
Give the person and number of a present indicative active and name its conjugation.
Recognise ten of the commonest verbs.
Recognise imperfect and future indicatives and parse them.
Recognise and parse the common forms of possum, eo, fero, volo, nolo and fio, and their compounds.
Recognise a perfect indicative active, parse it and connect it with its present.
Recognise ten more common verbs with their perfects.
Recognise pluperfect and future perfect indicatives.
Recognise passive forms of the present, imperfect and future and parse them.
Recognise the perfect passive participle and read it with sum as a perfect passive tense.
Recognise singular and plural imperatives, and negative commands.
Recognise present, perfect and passive infinitives.
Parse present, perfect and future participles and say whom they describe.
Recognise a deponent verb: passive in form, active in meaning.
Recognise ten common deponent verbs.
Parse third-declension adjectives of one, two and three endings, and i-stem nouns.
Parse the demonstrative pronouns and tell their senses apart.
Parse a relative pronoun and find its antecedent; recognise the interrogative quis, quid.
Read se and suus as referring to the subject, and tell suus from eius.
Recognise comparative and superlative forms, the two ways of saying 'than', and the formation of adverbs.
Read cardinal and ordinal numbers and decline unus, duo, tres and mille.
See the simple verb inside a compound, and read impersonal verbs such as oportet, licet and placet.
Recognise present and imperfect subjunctives and parse them.
Read a subjunctive in a main clause as a wish, an exhortation, a command or a doubt.
Recognise perfect and pluperfect subjunctives, active and passive.
Tell a purpose clause from a result clause and translate ut and ne accordingly.
Recognise an indirect command after a verb of asking or ordering, and an indirect question after a question word.
Tell the preposition cum from the conjunction, and read cum with the subjunctive as 'when', 'since' or 'although'.
Classify a condition by the mood and tense of its verbs and say what it supposes.
Explain why a subordinate subjunctive stands in the tense it does.
Read an accusative and infinitive as a reported statement and give the time of the infinitive relative to the main verb; read the Bible's quod, quia and quoniam clauses the same way.
Recognise an ablative absolute and translate it as a clause of time, cause, condition or concession.
Tell the gerund (a verbal noun) from the gerundive (a verbal adjective), and read ad + gerundive as purpose and the gerundive with sum as obligation.
Recognise the supine after verbs of motion and in set phrases, and the two periphrastic conjugations.
Read a relative clause with the subjunctive as describing a kind of person or thing, a purpose or a cause; and say how each clause of a sentence hangs on another.
Unpack a chain of participles and separated words in an Augustinian or classical period, and notice what the order emphasises.

Recognise the features the Vulgate owes to Hebrew and Greek: quia and quoniam for 'that', in with the ablative for instrument, the heavy use of participles, et at the head of every clause, and Hebrew idioms kept word for word.
Read a Psalm and a Gospel chapter in the Vulgate with reduced help.
Give the classical sense and the Christian use of ecclesia, baptismus, gratia, fides, caritas, salus, sacramentum, peccatum, gloria, spiritus, verbum and iustitia.
Read Cyprian's balanced, clear periods and Tertullian's compressed, abrupt ones.
Read the opening of the Confessions: prayer addressed to God in the second person, questions, antithesis, and the Psalms woven into the prose.
Plan the reading of a whole Latin work: set the assistance level, use the word panel and corpus occurrences sparingly, and keep a list of constructions to revisit.
Read the garden scene of Confessions 8 with only occasional help and follow its narrative and its argument.

topics.title: The Latin of the Bible and the Fathers

authoring.by: Written for Ecclesia by Claude (Anthropic), following the public-domain grammars listed as sources. Every Latin word shown as an example, in a paradigm or in an exercise is taken from the analysed editions in the library.
authoring.note: The explanations have not been reviewed by a Latinist. The linguistic analysis of every Latin text in the library is automatic: exercises use only words the analyser gave a single reading, and say so.
